entities.name: Arabic
entities.label: Idea
entities.summary:
Arabic, an Afro-Asiatic Semitic language, emerged from the Arabian Peninsula, with its earliest known inscriptions dating to the 4th century CE. It became the liturgical language of Islam with the revelation of the Quran to Prophet Muhammad in the 7th century, anchoring a vast religious and cultural sphere that stretched from the Atlantic to Central Asia. Beyond its sacred role, Arabic served as the primary vehicle for an unprecedented intellectual flourishing during the Islamic Golden Age, fundamentally shaping scientific, philosophical, and literary discourse across three continents for centuries.

The rapid expansion of the Rashidun and Umayyad Caliphates from 632 CE onward propelled Arabic far beyond its desert origins, establishing it as the administrative language of a new empire. This linguistic dominance fueled the Abbasid-era Translation Movement, notably centered at Baghdad's House of Wisdom (Bayt al-Hikma) from the 9th century, where thousands of Greek, Persian, and Indian texts were rendered into Arabic. Scholars like al-Kindi, al-Farabi, and Ibn Sina then built upon this foundation, producing original works in mathematics, medicine, astronomy, and philosophy that were disseminated throughout the Islamic world and beyond.

The profound legacy of Arabic manifested in its role as a lingua franca of scholarship and commerce, facilitating the transmission of knowledge from antiquity to medieval Europe, particularly through centers like Córdoba and Toledo. Its rich vocabulary and grammatical structures profoundly influenced numerous languages, including Persian, Turkish, Swahili, Urdu, and Spanish, contributing thousands of loanwords and shaping literary traditions. Modern Standard Arabic continues this tradition as one of the six official languages of the United Nations, spoken by over 420 million people worldwide, while its classical form remains the bedrock of Islamic theology and jurisprudence.
